Seller Representations Template (Corporate/Compliance): 'Status: duly incorporated... Capacity and Authority: has all requisite power... Non-violation: does not contravene... Insolvency: no Insolvency Event... Sanctions: not a Sanctioned Person... Data Protection: complied with Data Protection Laws...' — Standard due diligence reps. The Seller warrants it is a valid entity, compliant with laws (especially GDPR/Sanctions), and solvent. Breach triggers buyback or default.

Seller Receivables Representations Template: 'Eligible Receivables: each Purchased Receivable is an Eligible Receivable... Ownership: it owns... the entire interest... free of any Encumbrance... Valid and binding: constitute legal, valid and binding obligations... No Adverse Selection: no selection... on a basis which is adverse...' — Asset-level warranties. The core of the 'True Sale'. Seller guarantees the assets are what they say they are (valid, owned, unencumbered).

Seller Notification Undertakings: 'Notice of Litigation... Notice of Early Amortisation Event... Notice of Scottish/Northern Irish Receivable Recharacterisation Event... Notice of Account Bank Event...' — Information covenants. Seller must proactively tell the Trustee/Lenders if bad things happen (lawsuits, defaults, regulatory changes affecting the assets).

Security Trustee Appointment Clause: 'Each of the Secured Creditors appoints the Security Trustee to act as trustee... and authorises the Security Trustee to perform the duties... and to exercise the rights... [Trustee] shall hold the Secured Property... on trust for the benefit of the Secured Creditors...' — Establishes the trust structure. Essential for holding security for a changing group of lenders (fluctuating class). Trustee holds the bag (Security) so lenders don't have to retake it every time a bond trades.

Security Trustee Instructions & Discretion Clause: 'The Security Trustee shall... act on the instructions of the Instructing Creditor... [Trustee] may refrain from acting... until it has received any indemnification... [Trustee] shall have no duty to verify... [Trustee] shall not be liable... if it acts in accordance with instructions...' — Defensive drafting for the Trustee. It is an instruction-led entity, not a discretionary manager. It doesn't have to move unless told to and indemnified.

Supplement to Trustee Acts Clause: 'The statutory duty of care under section 1 of the Trustee Act 2000 shall not apply... [Trustee] may rely on advice... may appoint agents... shall not be bound to give notice... shall not be responsible for recitals...' — Disapplies statutory duties of care to provide higher protection to the commercial trustee. Allows reliance on experts and certificates without liability for verifying them.

Facility Agent Resignation & Replacement Clause: 'The Facility Agent may... resign... by giving [30] days’ notice... If a successor... has not been appointed... within [20] days... the Facility Agent may appoint a successor... The Senior Lenders... may... require the Facility Agent to resign...' — Mechanics for firing or quitting as Agent. Includes a 'force' appointment mechanism where if lenders don't pick a successor, the leaving Agent can pick one to ensure they can actually leave.

Erroneous Payment / Clawback Clause: 'If the Facility Agent pays an amount... and... notifies... that such payment was an Erroneous Payment then the Transaction Party... shall on demand refund the same... together with interest... [Payment] shall be made without set-off...' — Protects the Agent from 'fat finger' errors (like the Citibank/Revlon case). If the Agent sends money by mistake, recipients contractually agree to send it back immediately, overriding defenses like 'discharge for value'.

Deed of Accession Form (Schedule 11): '[ACCEDING_PARTY] agrees to become a party and to be bound by the terms of the Master Framework Agreement... as a [ROLE]. The Acceding Party is a company... [Administrative Details].' — The actual form used to add new parties (Swap Providers, etc.). Simple, standardized, ensuring new parties are instantly bound by the massive MFA structure.

Signing Page / Execution Block Template: 'EXECUTED as a DEED by [PARTY] acting by [SIGNATORY] in the presence of [WITNESS]...' — Standard execution blocks for English Law deeds. Requires witness signature for validity. Distinct blocks for Issuer, Seller, Trustees, Agents.

Tax Credit Benefit / Reimbursement Clause: 'If... the Issuer pays an additional amount [Gross-Up]... and the Affected Person... obtains a refund of Tax or credit... [and] is able to identify that... credit... that Affected Person shall reimburse the Issuer... such amount... that will leave it... in the same after-Tax position...' — Equity clause. If a lender gets a tax credit because the borrower paid their tax (via gross-up), they shouldn't keep both the gross-up and the credit. They must pay the credit back to the borrower to prevent unjust enrichment.

Expenses Reimbursement Clause (Post-Closing): 'The Issuer... shall indemnify and pay promptly on written demand each Affected Person in respect of all reasonable fees and out-of-pocket costs... incurred... after the Closing Date... in connection with: (a) consents, waivers or approvals... (b) amendments... (d) preservation or enforcement...' — Standard expense indemnity. Ensures lenders/agents aren't out of pocket for admin work, amendments, or enforcement actions requested by the Issuer or caused by defaults.

Interest on Unpaid Sums (Default Interest) Clause: 'If any Unpaid Sum... is not paid... on the due date... interest on the Unpaid Sum shall accrue... at the rate per annum which is the Transaction Default Rate... [typically Base Rate + Margin + 1-2%].' — Penal interest clause. Incentivizes timely payment and compensates creditors for the increased credit risk/cost of funds on overdue amounts.

Events of Default (Issuer) Template: 'Events of Default: (1) Principal non-payment... (2) Interest non-payment [Grace Period: 1 Day]... (6) Breach of Obligations [Grace Period: 3 Days]... (7) Misrepresentation... (9) Judgments... (14) Insolvency Event...' — Standard set of insolvency-remote SPV defaults. Tighter than corporate defaults (shorter grace periods) because SPVs are cashflow machines with no other business.

Back-up Servicer Event Trigger: 'No replacement following resignation of Back-up Servicer: if... Back-up Servicer resigns... and the Issuer fails to appoint any replacement... by the date on which the appointment... terminates.' — Critical structural protection. If the 'Spare Tire' (Back-up Servicer) quits and isn't replaced, the deal hits an Early Amortisation Event to protect investors from Servicer failure risk.

Seller Group Financial Covenants: 'Tangible Net Worth... less than GBP [AMOUNT]... Liquidity and Minimum Cash... less than GBP [AMOUNT]... Audited consolidated financial statements... not delivered...' — Corporate financial health triggers. Even though the deal is 'limited recourse', the Seller/Servicer needs minimum financial health to operate. Breach triggers Early Amortisation.

Security Trustee Exoneration (Reliance): 'The Security Trustee may call for and shall be at liberty to accept as sufficient evidence... a certificate of the Issuer signed by two directors... and shall not be bound in any such case to call for further evidence or be responsible for any loss...' — Standard trustee protection. Allows the trustee to rely on Issuer certificates (e.g., 'No Default is continuing') without needing to audit the Issuer itself.

Security Trustee Indemnification (Priority): 'The Security Trustee... shall be entitled to be indemnified out of the Secured Property and... may, in priority to any payment to the Senior Lenders... retain any part of any moneys... to effect such indemnity...' — Ensures the Trustee gets paid first. If the deal blows up, the Trustee takes its fees/costs from the enforcement proceeds before lenders get a penny.

Facility Agent Relationship with Lenders Clause: 'The Facility Agent may... treat the person shown in its records... as a Senior Lender... entitled to... payment... unless it has received notice... to the contrary.' — Administrative certainty. The Agent pays whoever is on the list. If lenders trade debt but don't tell the Agent, the Agent isn't liable for paying the old lender.

definitions.content: Master Framework Architecture and Incorporation: The Master Framework Agreement (MFA) serves as the central constitutional document for the securitization transaction. It establishes the 'Common Terms' (definitions, interpretation principles, and standard clauses) that are incorporated by reference into all other Transaction Documents (e.g., Senior Facility Agreement, Mezzanine Facility Agreement, Receivables Purchase Agreement). This architecture ensures semantic consistency across the entire suite of documents, reducing the risk of conflicting interpretations of key terms like 'Insolvency Event' or 'Business Day' across different agreements. By acting as a hub, it simplifies the accession process for new parties and centralizes the amendment process for universal terms.

Approved Electronic Money Institution: A regulatory status definition required for Account Banks within the structure. To qualify as an Approved Electronic Money Institution, an entity must be duly authorized for deposit-taking activities in its operating jurisdiction. If not an Electronic Money Institution, it must maintain minimum short-term unsecured credit ratings (P-1 by Moody’s, A-1 by S&P, F-1 by Fitch). If it is an Electronic Money Institution, it must meet specific approval criteria. This definition is critical for counterparty risk management, ensuring that Issuer funds (Collections and Reserves) are held only with institutions meeting high creditworthiness standards to prevent commingling or loss of funds.

Account Bank Event: A trigger event related to the financial health or regulatory status of the Issuer Account Bank or Collections Account Bank. It encompasses: (1) Insolvency Events or Proceedings; (2) for Electronic Money Institutions, specific insolvency definitions under Electronic Money Regulations 2011/99 or loss of authorization/registration; (3) an Account Bank Downgrade (falling below minimum rating requirements); or (4) a continuing breach or default under the Account Bank Agreement. Occurrence of this event typically forces the Issuer to replace the Account Bank within a specified cure period (e.g., 60-90 days) to protect transaction assets.

Available Distribution Amount (Pre-Enforcement): The aggregate pot of funds available on a Monthly Payment Date to pay secured creditors and expenses. It is calculated as the sum of: (1) credit balances in the Transaction Account, Issuer Collections Account, and Cash Reserve Account; (2) proceeds from Senior/Mezzanine Utilisation Requests intended for Receivable acquisition; (3) Swap receipts (excluding certain termination amounts); (4) Subordinated Facility advances (initially or for liquidity); and (5) enforcement proceeds (post-Security Enforcement Event). This definition determines the cash flow 'waterfall' capacity. It expressly excludes amounts advanced solely to credit the Pre-Funding Account or Cash Reserve Account to avoid double-counting.

Bail-In Legislation (Write-down and Conversion Powers): Refers to the statutory frameworks allowing regulators to rescue failing financial institutions by writing down debt or converting it to equity. Specifically includes Article 55 of the EU Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD) for EEA countries, the UK Bail-In Legislation for the UK, and analogous laws elsewhere. This definition is crucial for the 'Bail-In Acknowledgement' clause, where parties contractually recognize that their claims against a regulated entity (like an Account Bank or Swap Provider) may be statutorily reduced or converted by resolution authorities, overriding contractual payment terms.

Basic Term Modification: A comprehensive list of 'sacred rights' amendments that require 100% consent from all affected lenders (Senior and Mezzanine) rather than a simple majority. This includes changes to: (1) Maturity dates/Programme Scheduled Termination Date; (2) Currency of payment; (3) Principal/Interest amounts; (4) Priority of Payments; (5) Voting thresholds (Most Senior Lenders definition); (6) Borrowing Base definitions; (7) Eligibility Criteria or Concentration Limits (with specific exceptions); (8) Release of Security; and (9) Non-petition/Limited Recourse clauses. This definition protects minority creditors by preventing majority holders from altering the fundamental economic deal without universal agreement.

Borrowing Base Reporting Date: The precise timing deadline for the calculation of collateral value. Defined as 11:59 pm on the day prior (or two days prior) to the delivery of the Borrowing Base Report. For Monthly Servicer Reports, it refers to data available at 11:59 pm on the day (or two days) preceding the reporting date. This definition ensures the data used for calculating the Borrowing Base and Advance Rates is essentially 'fresh' but allows a strictly limited processing window (T-1 or T-2) for the Servicer to aggregate data. Accurate timing is vital to prevent gaming of the borrowing base by including/excluding assets around the cutoff.

Cash Reserve Target Amount: A liquidity protection mechanism defined dynamically based on the transaction stage. During the Revolving Period, it is set at 0.75% of the aggregate Senior Principal Amount Outstanding (accounting for daily fluctuations). After the Revolving Period ends, it steps down to zero (implying trapped cash is likely used to amortize debt or the reserve is no longer required in amortization phase). This reserve acts as a first line of defense against liquidity shortfalls for senior interest payments, ensuring timely payment even if collections are temporarily disrupted.

Collections: A broad, all-encompassing definition of cash flows derived from Purchased Receivables. It includes: (1) all finance charges and principal collections; (2) VAT (if any); (3) proceeds from Related Rights; (4) insurance proceeds; (5) Deemed Collections (amounts deemed received due to dilutions/set-off); (6) proceeds from the sale of Receivables to third parties; (7) Top-Up Receivable amounts paid to the Collections Account; (8) Swap receipts; and (9) Repurchase Prices paid by the Seller. This comprehensive definition ensures that all economic value flowing from the asset portfolio is captured within the securitization 'net' and applied through the Priority of Payments.

Defaulted Receivable: A Receivable status classification with three triggers: (1) unpaid for 90 days or more past due date; (2) identified by the Servicer as uncollectible or subject to write-off under Seller Policies; or (3) actually written off under Accounting Principles. This definition is binary and critical for the 'Borrowing Base' calculation, as Defaulted Receivables typically have zero value for funding purposes (Zero Advance Rate). The 90-day threshold is a standard regulatory (Basel/CRR) and rating agency benchmark for default.

Delinquent Receivable: A Receivable that is past due but not yet Defaulted. Defined as unpaid for 31 to 89 days (implied by the Defaulted definition of 90+ days). Crucially, this definition includes a 'Technical Failure Safe Harbor': a Receivable unpaid for 31+ days solely due to Employer Partner systems failure or reconciliation errors is NOT Delinquent, provided the failure is remedied within 31 days. This exception is specific to payroll-deduction lending (salary deduction), distinguishing administrative delays from genuine Borrower credit risk.

Encumbrance: A wide-reaching 'negative pledge' style definition covering any Security Interest, set-off arrangement, title transfer/retention, or preferential arrangement having the effect of security. The definition is drafted broadly to capture not just formal mortgages or charges, but any arrangement that would prioritize a third party over the Secured Creditors. This term is central to the 'No Encumbrances' representations and covenants given by the Seller and Issuer, ensuring the SPV has clean title to the assets.

Eligible Receivable: A Receivable that meets specific representations and warranties on its Purchase Date. Key characteristics include: (1) Ordinary course origination to an Employee; (2) Not Defaulted/Delinquent; (3) Fully disbursed (no future funding obligation); (4) Term 6-60 months; (5) Principal £250-£25,000; (6) Installment-to-income ratio ≤52%; (7) Payment via Salary Deduction (or Direct Debit/Push Payment if Employer has no deduction scheme); (8) Fixed interest 3.9%-34.9%; (9) Unsecured; (10) Validly assigned to Issuer; (11) No set-off/counterclaims; (12) Compliant with Consumer Credit Laws. Failure to meet these criteria usually triggers a Repurchase Obligation for the Seller.

Financial Indebtedness: A comprehensive definition of debt obligations used for covenant compliance. Includes: (a) borrowed money; (b) debit balances; (c) acceptance/discount facilities; (d) bond/note issuances; (e) finance leases; (f) sold/discounted receivables (recourse); (g) treasury/derivative transactions (mark-to-market value); (h) counter-indemnity obligations for guarantees/bonds; (i) redeemable shares; and (k) any transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing. This definition prevents the Issuer (or Seller, where applicable) from incurring off-balance sheet or disguised debt that could dilute the Senior Lenders' position.

Insolvency Event: A trigger covering various bankruptcy and distress scenarios for a Transaction Party (Seller, Servicer, Issuer). Includes: (a) dissolution; (b) inability to pay debts/insolvency admission; (c) general assignment for creditors; (d) institution of insolvency proceedings by regulators or self; (e) involuntary proceedings not dismissed within 30 days; (f) appointment of administrators/receivers; (g) secured party taking possession of assets (enforcement) not discharged within 30 days; or (h) analogous events in other jurisdictions. This is a standard 'Tripwire' definition; occurrence typically triggers Servicer Termination, Event of Default, or automatic Early Amortisation.

Instructing Creditor: The hierarchy of authority for directing the Security Trustee. (a) While Senior Commitments exist, it is the 'Majority Senior Lenders'; (b) If Seniors are paid out, it shifts to 'Mezzanine Note Purchasers' (66 2/3%); (c) If Mezzanine is paid out, it shifts to the 'Subordinated Lender'. This definition establishes the 'controlling class' concept, ensuring that the investors with the most senior risk exposure have control over enforcement and waivers. It prevents junior creditors from blocking enforcement actions required by senior creditors.

Legal Reservations: Standard legal qualifications limiting the absolute enforceability of Transaction Documents. Includes: (a) equitable remedies being discretionary; (b) limitation statutes time-barring claims; (c) possibility of recharacterization (fixed charge as floating, assignment as charge); (d) penalty clauses being void; (e) court discretion on costs; (f) prohibition on transfer voiding security over non-transferable contracts; and (g) conflict of laws regarding security over foreign assets. These reservations protect legal counsel and parties providing representations on enforceability by acknowledging inherent legal system limitations.

Material Adverse Effect (MAE): A broad catch-all definition for negative events triggering default. It covers material adverse effects on: (a) collectability of Receivables; (b) ability of Seller/Servicer/Issuer to perform material obligations; (c) legality/validity/enforceability of Transaction Documents or Security priority; (d) financial condition of the Seller/Servicer; or (e) rights/remedies of Senior Lenders/Mezzanine Purchasers. This is a subjective but powerful tool for lenders to call a default if the borrower's position deteriorates significantly in a way not captured by specific financial covenants.

Mezzanine Advance Rate: The borrowing limit percentage for the Mezzanine Facility against the asset pool. Defined as (a) 95% of Eligible Receivables (excluding Subprime); and (b) 70.5% for Subprime Receivables. This implies the Mezzanine sits between the Senior Advance Rate (likely lower) and these thresholds. The definition includes a dynamic adjustment mechanism where the Advance Rate is reduced by the 'Mezzanine Advance Rate Reduction Percentage' (5.0% or 2.5%) upon specific trigger events. It determines the maximum principal amount of Mezzanine Notes that can be issued against the portfolio.

Mezzanine Advance Rate Reduction Event: Triggers that lower the Mezzanine Advance Rate to protect lenders when portfolio quality deteriorates. Events include: (a) Direct Debit/Push Payment usage exceeding 19% (indicating deviation from the safer Salary Deduction model); (b) Default Rate > 1.25%; or (c) Default Rate > 0.75%. If (a) or (b) occurs, the rate reduces by 5.0%. If only (c) occurs, it reduces by 2.5%. This creates a dynamic collateralization mechanism where deterioration results in lower leverage and trapped cash (turbo-paydown).

Most Senior Lender Instruction: Defines the voting threshold for critical decisions. (a) While Original Senior Lender Group is involved: requires consent of the Original Senior Lender Group members. (b) If Original Group is gone: requires Senior Lenders holding > 66 2/3% of Senior Principal Amount. This definition gives the 'Original Senior Lender' (likely the arranging bank or anchor investor) a veto right or sole decision power during the Revolving Period, transitioning to a super-majority vote of lenders thereafter. It consolidates control in the hands of the primary funder.

Permitted Modification: A strict list of allowable changes to Borrower Agreements that do not trigger eligibility breaches or repurchase obligations. Includes: (a) minor/technical corrections; (b) changes required by law/regulation (FCA/ICO); (c) changes imposing tighter/conservative credit criteria; (d) changes consented to by the Facility Agent/Security Trustee; or (e) a 'Receivable Payment Date Change'. This definition balances the Servicer's operational need to manage loans (e.g., payroll dates changing) with the Lenders' need to prevent credit profile drift or loosening of terms.

Priority of Payments (Waterfall): The rigid, sequential order in which available funds are applied on each Monthly Payment Date. The Pre-Enforcement Waterfall order is generally: (1) Taxes/Trustee Fees; (2) Agent/Cash Manager Fees; (3) Corporate Services/Account Bank fees; (4) Swap Payments; (5) Issuer Profit; (6) Servicing Fees; (7) Senior Unused Fees; (8) Senior Interest; (9) Mezzanine Fees; (10) Mezzanine Interest; (11) Senior Principal; (12) Indemnities; (13) Cash Reserve Replenishment; (14) Swap Subordinated Amounts; (15) Mezzanine Interest (if Default); (16) Mezzanine Principal; (17) General Creditors; (18) Purchase Price for new receivables; (19) Subordinated Interest/Principal; (20) Deferred Purchase Price to Seller. This structure enforces the seniority of senior debt over mezzanine, and debt over equity/seller returns.

Programme Scheduled Termination Date: The expected maturity of the revolving commitment. Initially set as the date 36 months after the Closing Date (or 24 months if notified by Original Senior Lender). This date marks the end of the 'Revolving Period' (where principal is reinvested in new receivables) and the start of the 'Amortisation Period' (where principal is paid down). It can be extended via the 'Extension of Programme Scheduled Termination Date' mechanism, subject to Lender consent. Failure to pay by this date is not an immediate Event of Default, but failure to pay by the 'Final Maturity Date' is.

Qualifying Senior Lender: A tax status definition ensuring lenders are eligible to receive interest payments without UK withholding tax. Includes: (a) UK Tax Residents (companies/partnerships); (b) Non-residents trading through a UK Permanent Establishment; (c) Treaty Senior Lenders (residents of jurisdictions with a double taxation treaty with the UK granting full exemption); or (d) Building Societies. This definition is crucial for the 'Tax Gross Up' provisions; if a lender is NOT a Qualifying Senior Lender, the Issuer is typically not obliged to gross-up payments for withholding tax.

Related Rights: A comprehensive definition of all ancillary rights attaching to a Purchased Receivable. Includes: (a) guarantees, indemnities, and insurance policies; (b) rights to demand/sue for payment; (c) contractual rights against the Borrower; (d) rights against Employer Partners under Service Agreements (crucial for salary deduction loans); (e) all proceeds/collections; and (f) returned goods/repossessions. This ensures that when the Receivable is sold to the Issuer, the Issuer acquires not just the debt claim but the entire enforcement toolkit and security package associated with it.

Sanctioned Person: A strict compliance definition identifying prohibited counterparties. Includes: (a) persons listed on Sanctions Lists (OFAC, UN, EU, UK HMT); (b) governments of Sanctioned Countries; (c) persons operating/resident in Sanctioned Countries; or (d) persons owned/controlled by any of the above. This definition supports the 'Sanctions' representations and undertakings, ensuring the securitization proceeds are not used to fund illegal regimes or blocked persons, which would trigger regulatory fines and reputational damage for the Lenders.

Scottish Receivable Recharacterisation Event: A specific trigger event addressing legal risk in Scotland. It occurs if: (a) a court determines that a Receivable with a Scottish borrower must be governed by Scots law (despite being governed by English law in the contract); or (b) the Facility Agent determines such recharacterization is necessary to protect Secured Creditors. If this occurs, the Seller must execute 'Scottish Declarations of Trust' and 'Scottish Assignations in Security' to properly perfect the sale under Scots law. This highlights the jurisdictional complexity of UK securitizations where English and Scots law treat assignment and trust perfection differently.

Senior Advance Rate: The borrowing limit percentage for the Senior Facility. Defined as: (a) 84.5% for Eligible Receivables (excluding reduced rate buckets); (b) 60.0% for Subprime Reduced Advance Rate Concentration Amount; and (c) 77.5% for Near Prime Reduced Advance Rate Concentration Amount. Like the Mezzanine rate, this is the primary 'Loan-to-Value' (LTV) constraint for the senior debt. It ensures that there is always an equity/mezzanine cushion of at least 15.5% (100% - 84.5%) for prime assets, and significantly more (40%) for subprime assets, protecting senior lenders from first losses.

Senior Advance Rate Reduction Event: Triggers that lower the Senior Advance Rate to enforce deleveraging. Occurs if: (a) Direct Debit/Push Payment usage > 19% (deviation from Salary Deduction); or (b) Default Rate > 1.25%. If triggered, the Senior Advance Rate is reduced by the 'Senior Advance Rate Reduction Percentage'. This mechanism works identically to the Mezzanine equivalent but protects the Senior class. It correlates leverage directly to asset performance—worse performance equals lower allowable debt.

Senior Borrowing Base: The calculation determining the maximum allowable Senior Principal Amount Outstanding. It is the sum of: (1) Senior Net Eligible Receivables Balance multiplied by the (adjusted) Senior Advance Rate; plus (2) Cash in Transaction/Collections/Pre-Funding Accounts. If the Senior Principal exceeds this base (a 'Borrowing Base Breach'), the Issuer cannot draw further funds and must cure the breach (usually by repaying debt or adding assets). This is the fundamental 'Asset Coverage Test' for the deal.

Senior Net Eligible Receivables Balance (Senior NERB): The adjusted value of the portfolio used for the Senior Borrowing Base. It starts with the total Eligible Receivables and subtracts 'Excess Concentration Amounts'. These excess amounts are specific portfolio concentrations that exceed agreed limits (e.g., too many Subprime borrowers, too much exposure to one Employer Partner). By deducting these excesses *before* applying the Advance Rate, the structure gives zero credit to assets breaching concentration limits, effectively penalizing the Issuer for unbalanced portfolios.

Swap Agreement: Specifically defined as an ISDA Master Agreement and Schedule entered into by the Issuer to hedge interest rate risk (specifically the mismatch between fixed-rate Receivables and floating-rate Senior Notes/Facilities). The definition includes a 'Coverage Requirement' (90%-110% of Senior Principal). It captures the economic transfer of risk without transferring asset ownership. This is critical for the 'Fixed-Floating' mismatch inherent in the deal. The Swap Provider usually ranks high in the Priority of Payments (senior to principal) to ensure the hedge remains in place.

Subordinated Lender Repayment Amount: The amount available to pay the Subordinated Lender (equity piece) after all senior obligations are met. It is calculated as the *lower* of: (a) Subordinated Principal Outstanding; or (b) the 'Excess' amount remaining after calculating the borrowing base requirements and paying senior items. This mechanism effectively traps cash. If an Early Amortisation Event occurs, this amount drops to zero (turbo-paydown of senior) until senior debt is fully repaid. This defines the 'equity return' mechanics and the subordination structure.

Tangible Net Worth: A financial covenant definition for the Seller/Guarantor. Defined as the aggregate book equity of the Seller Group entities, *excluding* intangible assets (goodwill, IP), but *adding back* specific intercompany loans (e.g., loans from Salary Direct Holdings or ELQ Investors). This adjusted metric focuses on hard asset value available to support the Seller's buy-back obligations and servicing duties. A breach of the Tangible Net Worth floor (e.g., falling below £35m or £17.5m depending on profit conditions) triggers a 'Seller Group Event', potentially leading to default.

Transaction Documents: The definitive list of all contracts constituting the securitization. Includes: Master Framework Agreement, Senior/Mezzanine/Subordinated Facility Agreements, Receivables Purchase Agreement, Servicing Agreement, Security Agreement, Scottish Declarations/Assignations, Swap Agreements, Account Bank Agreements, Corporate Services Agreement, Fee Letters, and Powers of Attorney. This definition is vital for the 'Event of Default' clause (breach of *any* Transaction Document) and the 'Entire Agreement' concept. It binds the disparate parts of the structure into a single legal ecosystem.

VAT (Value Added Tax): Defined broadly to include UK VAT (Value Added Tax Act 1994), EU VAT (Directive 2006/112), and any similar tax. The definition is crucial for the 'VAT Gross Up' and 'Reverse Charge' clauses. The agreement specifies that all payments are deemed exclusive of VAT; if VAT is chargeable, the payer must pay an additional amount equal to the VAT. This protects the net economic return to the Lenders and Service Providers. Specific 'Reverse Charge' mechanics apply where the recipient accounts for VAT, ensuring tax neutrality where possible.

Unpaid Sum: Any amount (principal, interest, fees) that is due and payable but not paid on the due date. The agreement imposes a specific interest penalty on Unpaid Sums: they accrue interest at the 'Transaction Default Rate' (Senior/Mezzanine Rate + 2.00%). This penalty interest capitalizes/compounds if not paid. This definition acts as a strong economic incentive for timely payment and compensates lenders for the distress/holding cost of defaulted amounts.

Transaction Default Rate: The penalty interest rate applied to Unpaid Sums. Defined as the base interest rate (Senior Interest Rate or Mezzanine Note Interest Rate) *plus* a margin of 2.00%. This 'surge pricing' reflects the increased credit risk of a borrower (Issuer) that has missed payments. It applies automatically to any overdue amounts under the Senior or Mezzanine facilities.

Concentration Limit: A set of portfolio composition limits that, if breached, reduce the Borrowing Base (via the 'Excess Concentration Amount' deduction). Limits include: (1) Max 50 months Weighted Average Remaining Term; (2) Weighted Average APR > Swap Rate + 9.5%; (3) Single Employer Partner cap (20-25%); (4) Top Five Employer Partners cap (50%); (5) Direct Debit/Push Payment cap (19% / 3.5%); (6) Adjusted Loan Terms caps (12% Prime, 4% Near Prime); (7) Subprime Borrower cap (20%). These limits enforce diversity and credit quality, ensuring the pool doesn't drift into riskier segments (e.g., too much subprime, too much single-employer concentration).

Subprime Borrower: A Borrower classification based on credit score. Defined as a borrower with a 'Gauge 2 Score' ≤ 550 and a 'Delphi 11SBN Score' ≤ 610. This definition is used to segment the portfolio for Advance Rates (Subprime gets a lower advance rate of 70.5% vs 95% for Prime) and Concentration Limits (capped at 20% of pool). Precise scoring thresholds allow for objective, data-driven risk segmentation.

Near Prime Borrower: A Borrower classification sitting between Prime and Subprime. Defined as a borrower with a 'Gauge 2 Score' between 551-590 and a 'Delphi 11SBN Score' between 611-790. Like Subprime, this category likely attracts specific concentration limits or advance rate adjustments (though primarily defined to distinguish from the Prime and Subprime buckets).

Prime Borrower: The highest credit quality borrower segment. Defined as a borrower with a 'Gauge 2 Score' of at least 591 and a 'Delphi 11SBN Score' of at least 791. Assets from these borrowers attract the highest Advance Rates (up to 95%) and are the preferred collateral type. This definition sets the 'Gold Standard' for the portfolio.

Salary Deduction: A specific payment method where the Borrower's loan repayment is deducted directly from their salary by their Employer Partner (payroll deduction) before the net salary is paid to the Borrower. This is the primary/preferred payment method for this transaction (Neyber model). It reduces credit risk significantly compared to Direct Debit, as payment priority is higher. Receivables NOT paid by Salary Deduction (i.e., Direct Debit/Push Payment) are subject to strict caps (19%) and higher haircuts (Advance Rate Reduction), reflecting their higher risk.

Employer Partner: A corporate entity that has entered into a service agreement with the Seller to facilitate Salary Deduction loans for its employees. The credit risk of the portfolio is partly linked to these Employers (counterparty risk). Concentration Limits apply to 'Single Employer Partner' and 'Top Five Employer Partners' to prevent the portfolio performance from being too dependent on the solvency of a few large companies handling the payroll deductions.

Technical Failure (Safe Harbor): A specific carve-out in the Delinquency definition. If a payment is missed solely due to an Employer Partner's systems failure or reconciliation error (not borrower default), it is NOT counted as Delinquent for 31 days. This recognises that in Salary Deduction lending, a 'missed payment' might just mean the Employer's payroll software had a glitch or the bulk transfer was delayed. Without this definition, operational hiccups at Employers would trigger massive default reporting and potential Early Amortisation, falsely indicating credit deterioration.

Security Trustee Indemnification: A comprehensive protection mechanism for the Security Trustee. The Trustee is not required to act (even on instructions) unless 'indemnified and/or secured and/or pre-funded to its satisfaction'. The Issuer indemnifies the Trustee against all Liabilities, costs, and expenses (including legal fees and VAT) incurred in the execution of its duties, except in cases of gross negligence, willful misconduct, or fraud. This indemnity is secured by the Transaction Security and ranks top of the Priority of Payments ('super-senior'), ensuring the Trustee is always paid first, incentivizing them to act without fear of personal financial loss.

Limited Recourse: A fundamental securitization provision limiting the Issuer's liability to its assets. Secured Creditors agree that their recourse against the Issuer is limited to the 'Available Funds' and the 'Secured Property'. If, after enforcement and application of proceeds via the waterfall, there is a shortfall, that shortfall is extinguished. Creditors cannot sue the Issuer for the balance or petition for its winding-up (Non-Petition). This ensures the Issuer constitutes a 'bankruptcy remote' vehicle, isolating the assets from the insolvency of the Originator or the creditors themselves.

Break Costs: The cost incurred by a Lender if the Issuer repays principal on a date *other* than a Monthly Payment Date (or a scheduled Interest Payment Date). It represents the cost of unwinding funding arrangements or redeploying funds (often related to LIBOR/SONIA match-funding or breakage of underlying swaps). The Issuer indemnifies Lenders for these costs. This definition ensures Lenders receive their expected yield-to-maturity (or period) without penalty for the Borrower's prepayment decisions.

Tax Gross-Up (Withholding Tax): A provision requiring the Issuer (or Seller) to pay additional amounts if a 'Tax Deduction' (withholding) is required by law on payments to Lenders. If the Issuer must withhold X%, it must pay Y% more so the Lender receives the full intended amount. Crucially, this does *not* apply to 'FATCA Deductions' (which are carved out) or if the Lender is not a 'Qualifying Senior Lender' (e.g., a tax resident of a non-treaty jurisdiction). This allocates change-of-law tax risk to the Issuer/structure rather than the Lender.

Erroneous Payment: A provision addressing operational errors by the Facility Agent (e.g., accidentally paying the wrong lender or the wrong amount). If the Agent determines a payment was made in error, the recipient is legally obliged to refund it on demand, plus interest (cost of funds). The clause explicitly states that an Erroneous Payment does NOT discharge the Issuer's underlying debt obligation (i.e., the debt isn't 'paid' just because the Agent sent money by mistake). This protects the Agent from operational losses and prevents unjust enrichment of recipients.

Standstill Period (Enforcement): A restrictive covenant preventing the Security Trustee (and Mezzanine lenders) from enforcing security immediately upon an Event of Default if directed by Junior creditors. Specifically, if the Senior Lenders instruct enforcement, the Mezzanine Agent has a consultation right (2-5 days) but cannot block it. If Mezzanine Lenders want to enforce when Seniors do not, they are often blocked ('Standstill') for a specific period to allow the Senior Lenders to control the process. This ensures orderly liquidation and prevents junior creditors from destroying value for senior creditors through premature enforcement.

Option to Purchase (Senior Loans): A call option granted to Mezzanine Note Purchasers. Upon a Senior Event of Default or Enforcement Notification, the Mezzanine holders have the right to purchase *all* (not part) of the Senior Loans at par (plus accrued interest/costs). This allows Mezzanine lenders to buy out the controlling Senior class, terminate the enforcement/standstill, and take control of the workout process themselves. This is a standard 'Equity Cure' or 'Buyout' right in leveraged finance structures.
